title: Plate Boundaries
description: Earth's crust is in pieces — and they move

concepts.title: The Theory of Plate Tectonics
concepts.contentHtml:
Earth's outer shell — the lithosphere — is broken into about 15 large slabs called tectonic plates. They float on the slowly flowing mantle below.

The plates move at roughly the speed your fingernails grow — a few centimeters per year. Slow, but over millions of years they reshape continents.

This theory was only accepted in the 1960s. Before that, Alfred Wegener's 1912 idea of continental drift was ridiculed — until ocean-floor mapping revealed the spreading ridges that made the mechanism undeniable.

concepts.title: Three Boundary Types
concepts.contentHtml:
Plates meet in three ways:

Divergent — plates move apart. Magma rises to fill the gap, creating new crust. The mid-Atlantic Ridge is widening the Atlantic by ~2.5 cm/year.

Convergent — plates collide. The denser one usually slides under (subduction); if both are continental, neither sinks and they crumple into mountains.

Transform — plates slide past each other horizontally. California's San Andreas Fault is the classic example.

concepts.title: What Drives the Plates
concepts.contentHtml:
The mantle isn't liquid, but over geological time it flows like extremely thick honey. Heat from Earth's core drives convection currents: hot mantle rises, cools, and sinks, dragging plates along.

Two forces matter most:

Ridge push — gravity slides plates away from raised mid-ocean ridges.
Slab pull — at subduction zones, the dense sinking plate yanks the rest along behind it.

Slab pull is now thought to be the dominant force. Plates aren't just passengers on convection — they help drive it.

title: Earthquakes & Mountains
description: What happens when plates push, pull, and slip

concepts.title: Stress, Strain, and Faults
concepts.contentHtml:
Rocks under tectonic forces accumulate stress (force per area) and deform — that deformation is strain.

Rocks behave elastically up to a point. Past that point, they fracture along a fault. The two sides of a fault store enormous energy as they bend before snapping.

The release of that stored elastic energy is an earthquake. The point where rupture begins is the focus; the point on the surface directly above is the epicenter.

concepts.title: Measuring Earthquakes
concepts.contentHtml:
Earthquake size is measured on a magnitude scale (the modern one is moment magnitude, often loosely called Richter).

The scale is logarithmic: each whole number is 10× the ground motion and roughly 32× the energy. A magnitude 7 quake releases ~32× more energy than a magnitude 6, and ~1000× more than a 5.

This is why a magnitude 9 quake (like Tōhoku 2011) is catastrophic and a 5 is barely felt — the difference is ten thousand times the energy.

concepts.title: How Mountains Form
concepts.contentHtml:
Most mountain ranges form at convergent boundaries:

— The Himalayas are still rising as India crashes into Asia at ~5 cm/year. Both plates are continental, neither sinks, and the crust crumples upward.
— The Andes formed because the oceanic Nazca plate subducts beneath South America, melting and pushing magma up to build volcanoes along the spine.
— The Appalachians are old and worn down — once Himalayan-scale, now eroded across hundreds of millions of years.

Mountains are temporary. Erosion always wins, eventually.

title: Volcanoes & Hotspots
description: How magma reaches the surface — sometimes spectacularly

concepts.title: Where Magma Comes From
concepts.contentHtml:
Most magma forms at plate boundaries:

— At subduction zones, water from the descending plate lowers the mantle's melting point, generating wet, gas-rich magma.
— At divergent ridges, decompression melts the rising mantle.
— At hotspots, isolated plumes of mantle rise from deep within Earth.

Each source produces magma with distinct chemistry — and very different volcanic behavior. Subduction-zone magma is sticky and gas-laden, leading to explosive eruptions; ridge magma is runny and quiet.

concepts.title: Three Types of Volcanoes
concepts.contentHtml:
Shield volcanoes — broad, gentle slopes from runny basaltic lava. Hawaii's Mauna Loa is the largest mountain on Earth by volume. Eruptions are usually safe to watch from a distance.

Stratovolcanoes (composite) — steep, classic cone shape from alternating ash and lava. Mount Fuji, Vesuvius, Mount St. Helens. These are the dangerous ones — explosive, unpredictable, deadly.

Cinder cones — small, steep, made of loose volcanic gravel. Often form in single eruptive events lasting weeks to years.

concepts.title: Hotspots — The Anomalies
concepts.contentHtml:
Most volcanoes occur at plate boundaries — but some erupt smack in the middle of plates.

These hotspots are fueled by isolated mantle plumes that stay roughly fixed while plates drift overhead. As the plate moves, the plume punches a chain of volcanoes through it.

The Hawaiian Islands are the textbook example — an active volcano (Kīlauea) at one end, extinct islands trailing northwest, all from the same hotspot. Yellowstone is a continental hotspot, sitting under thick crust and producing supervolcano eruptions every ~600,000 years.

title: Earth's Interior
description: The hidden layers below our feet

concepts.title: Crust, Mantle, Core
concepts.contentHtml:
Earth has four main layers:

— Crust — thin rocky shell, 5–70 km thick. Oceanic crust is denser; continental is thicker.
— Mantle — solid but flowing rock to ~2,900 km. Source of magma, driver of plate tectonics.
— Outer core — molten iron and nickel, 2,200 km thick.
— Inner core — solid iron-nickel ball, 1,200 km radius. Despite being hottest of all, pressure keeps it solid.

The deepest hole ever drilled (Kola Superdeep, 12 km) didn't even reach the mantle. Everything below is inferred indirectly.

concepts.title: How We Know — Seismic Waves
concepts.contentHtml:
We can't dig down. But earthquake waves travel through Earth and behave differently in different materials.

P-waves (compression) travel through solid AND liquid.
S-waves (shear) only travel through solid.

S-waves DON'T appear on the far side of Earth from a quake — there's a 'shadow zone'. This proved the outer core must be liquid.

Wave speeds, refraction, and reflection let us map the interior layer by layer. Every earthquake is a free CT scan of the planet.

concepts.title: The Magnetic Field
concepts.contentHtml:
Earth's magnetic field is generated by convection in the molten outer core. Iron-rich fluid moving in a self-sustaining dynamo produces our planet's magnetic shield.

The field protects us from solar wind that would otherwise strip the atmosphere — Mars lost most of its atmosphere this way after its core froze and its magnetic field died.

The field also flips on roughly half-million-year timescales — the magnetic north and south swap positions. The last full reversal was 780,000 years ago. We're overdue, but flips take thousands of years and aren't catastrophic.

title: How We Got the Theory
description: From Wegener's ridicule to scientific consensus

concepts.title: Wegener's Continental Drift (1912)
concepts.contentHtml:
Alfred Wegener, a German meteorologist, noticed in 1912 that the coasts of Africa and South America fit together like puzzle pieces. He proposed that the continents were once joined as a supercontinent — Pangaea — and have since drifted apart.

He gathered impressive evidence: matching fossils across oceans, identical rock formations on different continents, glacial scratches that lined up across modern continents.

His evidence was strong. His mechanism was wrong — and that doomed the theory for half a century.

concepts.title: Why Geologists Rejected It
concepts.contentHtml:
Wegener's proposed mechanism — continents 'plowing' through ocean crust — was physically impossible. Mainstream geologists rightly objected.

For 50 years, continental drift was treated as crank science. Wegener died on a Greenland expedition in 1930 still defending it. Geology textbooks dismissed his ideas through the 1950s.

The lesson: strong evidence isn't enough. Without a plausible mechanism, even correct theories struggle for acceptance. Lord Kelvin had the same problem when he calculated Earth's age from cooling — he was wrong, but his physics was unanswerable until radioactivity was discovered.

concepts.title: Vindication — Seafloor Spreading
concepts.contentHtml:
In the 1960s, ocean-floor mapping revealed two stunning facts:

1. The mid-ocean ridges are where new crust forms, spreading outward.
2. Magnetic reversals are recorded as symmetric stripes on either side of the ridges.

The stripes were the smoking gun: ocean floor moves like a conveyor belt outward from ridges. Continents don't 'plow' — they're carried passively on plates that include ocean and continent together.

Wegener was right. He just didn't live to see it. By the late 1960s, plate tectonics was the unifying theory of the Earth sciences — geology's analog of evolution or atomic theory.
